content: Certainly. 1. Usizoka M, Baisley K, et al. conducted a study examining the factors associated with HIV-1 genital shedding in Tanzanian women, published in PLoS One in 2011. The findings provide insights into the virological and immunological dynamics of HIV in the female genital tract. 2. Heikinheimo O, Lehtovirta P, Aho I, Ristola M, and Paavonen J. performed a 5-year follow-up study on the use of the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system in women infected with HIV. Their research, published in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology, highlights the safety and efficacy of this contraceptive method in this population. 3. Aweeka FT, Rosenkranz SL, Segal Y, Coombs RW, Bardeguez A, Thevanayagam L, et al. investigated the impact of sex and contraceptive therapy on the pharmacokinetics of zidovudine in plasma and intracellular compartments. Their study, published in AIDS in 2006, provides critical data on how these factors influence antiretroviral drug levels. 4. Kearney BP and Mathias A. demonstrated that tenofovir disoproxil fumarate does not alter the pharmacokinetics of hormonal contraceptives. This study, published in Pharmacotherapy in 2009, reassures clinicians about the compatibility of these medications. 5. Landolt NK, Phanuphak N, Ubolyam S, Pinyakorn S, Kriengsinyot R, Ahluwalia J, et al. found that efavirenz, unlike nevirapine, negatively affects progesterone and antiretroviral levels when co-administered with combined oral contraceptives. This study, published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2013, underscores the need for careful consideration of drug interactions in HIV-infected women. 6. Mildvan D, Yarrish R, Marshak A, Hutman HW, McDonough M, Lamson M, et al. explored the pharmacokinetic interaction between nevirapine and ethinyl estradiol/norethindrone in HIV-infected women. Their findings, published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, provide valuable guidance for managing concurrent use of these medications. 7. Nanda K, Delany-Moretlwe S, Dube K, Lendvay A, Kwok C, Molife L, et al. reported that nevirapine-based antiretroviral therapy does not compromise the effectiveness of oral contraceptives. This study, published in AIDS in 2013, supports the continued use of oral contraceptives in women on this regimen. 8. Stuart GS, Moses A, Corbett A, Phiri G, Kumwenda W, Mkandawire N, et al. examined the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of combined oral contraceptives and generic antiretroviral formulations in Malawian women. Their study, published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2011, provides region-specific data on drug interactions. 9. Carten ML, Kiser JJ, Kwara A, Mawhinney S, Cu-Uvin S. investigated the pharmacokinetic interactions between the emergency contraceptive levonorgestrel (Plan B) and efavirenz. Their findings, published in Infectious Diseases in Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2012, highlight potential concerns for women using both medications. 10. Sevinsky H, Eley T, Persson A, Garner D, Yones C, Nettles R, et al. studied the effect of efavirenz on the pharmacokinetics of an oral contraceptive containing ethinyl estradiol and norgestimate in healthy HIV-negative women. Their research, published in Antiviral Therapy in 2011, provides important insights into drug interactions in this context. 11. Crauwels HM, van Heeswijk RP, Buelens A, Stevens M, Hoetelmans RM. demonstrated that rilpivirine does not affect the pharmacokinetics of ethinyl estradiol and norethindrone in healthy volunteers. This study, published in the International Journal of Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics in 2014, supports the compatibility of these drugs. 12. Scholler-Gyure M, Kakuda TN, Woodfall B, Aharchi F, Peeters M, Vandermeulen K, et al. evaluated the effect of steady-state etravirine on the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of ethinyl estradiol and norethindrone. Their findings, published in Contraception in 2009, provide reassurance about the safety of this combination. 13. Perry SH, Swamy P, Preidis GA, Mwanyumba A, Motsa N, Sarero HN. addressed concerns about drug interactions leading to unintended pregnancies when implementing the Jadelle implant in HIV-infected women in sub-Saharan Africa. Their study, published in AIDS in 2014, highlights the importance of monitoring and managing such interactions. 14. Cohn SE, Park JG, Watts DH, Stek A, Hitti J, Clax PA, et al. found that depot-medroxyprogesterone acetate provides effective contraception without clinically significant interactions with antiretroviral therapy. This study, published in Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics in 2007, supports its use in HIV-infected women. 15. Nanda K, Amaral E, Hays M, Viscola MA, Mehta N, Bahamondes L. investigated the pharmacokinetic interactions between depot medroxyprogesterone acetate and combination antiretroviral therapy. Their findings, published in Fertility and Sterility in 2008, provide critical data for clinical decision-making. 16. Vogler MA, Patterson K, Kamemoto L, Park JG, Watts H, Aweeka F, et al. assessed the contraceptive efficacy of oral and transdermal hormones when co-administered with protease inhibitors in HIV-1-infected women. Their study, published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2010, offers valuable insights into contraceptive management in this population. 17. Atrio J, Stanczyk FZ, Neely M, Cherala G, Kovacs A, Mishell DR Jr. evaluated the effect of protease inhibitors on the steady-state pharmacokinetics of oral norethindrone contraception in HIV-infected women. Their findings, published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2014, provide guidance for clinicians managing these patients. 18. Anderson MS, Hanley WD, Moreau AR, Jin B, Bieberdorf FA, Kost JT, et al. studied the effect of raltegravir on the pharmacokinetics of estradiol and norgestimate following oral contraceptive administration in healthy women. Their research, published in the British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology in 2011, supports the compatibility of these medications. 19. Song I, Mark S, Borland J, Chen S, Wajima T, Peppercorn A, et al. demonstrated that dolutegravir does not affect the pharmacokinetics of methadone or oral contraceptives containing norgestimate and ethinyl estradiol. This study, accessed in 2014, provides reassurance about the safety of these combinations.
